newsitem.title: USA: Weekly jobless claims down in latest week.
newsitem.headline: Weekly jobless claims down in latest week.

text.p: The number of Americans seeking new unemployment benefits fell last week, the government said on Thursday.

The Labour Department said state jobless claims in the week ended March 8 fell to 307,000 from a revised 312,000 the week before. Wall Street economists had forecast initial jobless claims of 313,000.
The four-week moving average -- which economists regard as a better gauge because it flattens out weekly volatility -- fell to 310,250 from a revised 310,500 the previous week.

The department said the total number of Americans on benefit rolls dropped to 2,335,000 in the week ended March 1, the latest week for which that data are available. That was the lowest level since May 7, 1990, when claims hit 2,317,000.
The department said five states reported decreases in claims exceeding 1,000 on an unadjusted basis in the week ended March 1, the latest period for which that data are available.
They were Massachusetts with 4,126, Texas with 2,166, Michigan with 2,119, Rhode Island with 1,359 and Connecticut with 1,173.

Texas said it had fewer layoffs in the service industry, Michigan reported fewer layoffs in various industries and Rhode Island reported fewer layoffs in the trade and service industries and in manufacturing.
Massachusetts and Connecticut gave no reason for the drop in claims.

There were five states reporting increases in claims exceeding 1,000 in the March 1 week. They were New York with 8,320, Arkansas with 1,694, Ohio with 1,509, New Jersey with 1,197 and Illinois with 1,184.

New York linked its increase to the return to the five-day work week after a shorter reporting period the week before due to the Presidents Day holiday. It also reported layoffs in various industries. Arkansas had layoffs in the food and transportation equipment industries.
New Jersey and Illinois both reported layoffs in the trade and service industries and in manufacturing. Ohio had no comment.
